analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock mining companies an 8% royalty and cleanup fees to reclaim abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: A bill to make hardrock miners pay royalties for public-land minerals and fund cleanup of abandoned mines was introduced with 30 Democratic cosponsors, referred to two committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining (gold, copper, silver and similar metals) is still governed by an 1872 law that lets companies take minerals from federal land without paying any royalty to the government. This bill would charge an 8% royalty on the gross income from mining on federal claims, charge an annual fee for each claim held, and require companies to post bonds covering the full cost of cleaning up a mine site. The money would flow into a fund to reclaim tens of thousands of abandoned mines that pollute western streams and threaten drinking water, and it would help volunteers who clean up old mines without being sued. The bill never got a single hearing or vote; it died in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines, which are the main losers under the current system: abandoned hardrock mines leach acid and heavy metals into streams, and the public typically ends up paying for cleanup. The bill would direct mining royalties and per-ton fees into a fund for reclaiming abandoned sites and for community impact assistance in mining areas. It would also protect watersheds, national parks, and tribal cultural sites by letting states, local governments, and tribes petition to close specific federal lands to mining, and it would shield Good Samaritan volunteers from Clean Water Act liability when they clean up old mines.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an 8% royalty on the gross income from hardrock minerals produced on federal mining claims, with the money deposited into a new Hardrock Minerals Fund [S2] [S3].
Charges operators a 7-cent-per-ton fee on displaced rock and ore, deposited into the same fund, to pay for reclaiming land and water damaged by past hardrock mining [S2] [S3].

Requires operations permits with financial assurance sufficient to cover full reclamation and any long-term water treatment, and requires mined land to be restored to a condition capable of supporting prior or other beneficial uses [S2] [S3].

Lets any state, local government, or Indian tribe petition the Interior Secretary to withdraw specific federal land from mining to protect drinking water watersheds, wildlife habitat, or tribal religious and cultural values, with the petition granted unless the Secretary publishes findings that granting it would be against the national interest [S2] [S3].

Includes a Good Samaritan title that shields people with no role in creating historic mine pollution from Clean Water Act liability if they clean up abandoned mines under an approved discharge permit [S2] [S3].

Exempts small operators — those with less than $100,000 in annual gross mineral income and no more than 10 claims — from both the royalty and the reclamation fee, so small prospectors are not priced out [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, which today pay no production royalty: they would owe an 8% royalty on gross income (4% for mines already operating under a permit), a $200 annual fee per claim held, and a 7-cent-per-ton reclamation fee, plus the cost of posting full-cleanup financial assurance before operations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: The 8% royalty on gross income and the per-claim and per-ton fees would raise costs for companies mining federal land, and industry opponents of such measures have long argued this discourages domestic mineral production; the bill partially offsets this by cutting the rate to 4% for mines already operating under a permit and exempting small producers [S2] [S3].

The permit, reclamation-plan, and financial-assurance requirements add significant regulatory steps and upfront bonding costs before mining can begin, which favors large companies with the resources to comply over small ones [S3].
The bill channels judicial review of the rules implementing the Act to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, limiting where affected parties can challenge the regulations [S2].
Grandfathering cuts the royalty to 4% for existing producing mines, a concession that reduces revenue from exactly the largest, most profitable operations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: it would end the only major extractive industry that still pays no federal production royalty on public-land minerals, and use the revenue to address a cleanup liability — abandoned mines polluting western waters — that currently falls on taxpayers. The costs fall on a specific industry and would partly pass through to mineral prices; the concessions to existing mines and the small-operator exemptions blunt both the industry's burden and the bill's revenue. The Good Samaritan title is a widely supported fix that would ease cleanups regardless of the rest of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Natural Resources and Transportation and Infrastructure committees, then to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on February 13, 2015, and it was referred to the Committee on Natural Resources and, in addition, to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1] [S3] [S5].
Within days it was sent to subcommittees: the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee on February 17, 2015, and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on March 16, 2015 [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].
All 30 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: the bill's death preserved the status quo in which they extract gold, copper, and other minerals from federal land without paying any production royalty, while the cleanup costs of abandoned mines remain with taxpayers and downstream communities.

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Hardrock Mining Reform and Reclamation Act of 2015.

for.name: 30 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 30 recorded cosponsors were Democrats, including original cosponsors such as Reps. DeFazio, Huffman, and Blumenauer.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee shared jurisdiction over the bill and likewise never acted on it after the February 2015 referral.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Gold, copper, and other hardrock producers on federal land
against.what_they_did: The mining industry has long opposed federal hardrock royalties and reclamation fees of this kind, and Republicans on the Natural Resources Committee — which holds jurisdiction over mining law — made no move to advance the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no votes, so no roll-call record exists, but support was entirely Democratic — Grijalva and 30 Democratic cosponsors — and the Republican-controlled committees never acted on it.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver, etc.)
industries.note: These companies currently mine gold, copper, and other hardrock minerals from federal land under an 1872 law that charges no production royalty; the bill would impose an 8% royalty, annual claim fees, a per-ton reclamation fee, and full-cleanup bonding. Their interest in keeping public-land mining royalty-free runs directly against the taxpayers who cover abandoned-mine cleanup. [S2] [S3]

Claimants holding ten or fewer claims who perform assessment work are exempt from the $200 annual maintenance fee, and producers with under $100,000 in gross mineral income are exempt from both the royalty and the reclamation fee — so the burden falls on larger operators, not hobbyists. [S3]

industries.industry: Mine reclamation and environmental remediation contractors
industries.note: The Hardrock Reclamation Account would fund cleanup of abandoned mine lands, creating paid reclamation work; the Good Samaritan title would also remove a legal barrier that currently deters cleanup projects. [S2]
